Philasande's mechanical heart

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
a ten year old boy becomes the first child in the world to be fitted with the life saving mechanical heart.

Unique Selling Point:
Philasande Dladla became the first child on the African continent to undergo a lifesaving operation where a “mechanical heart” was implanted to assist his damaged heart.

He is also the first child in the world to have a mechanical heart implanted in him.

Doctors at the Netcare Christiaan Barnard Memorial Hospital in Cape Town inserted a heart ventricular assist device (HVAD) in Dladla aged 10 from KwaZulu-Natal.

Dr Willie Koen, a cardiac and transplant surgeon practising at the hospital, and a founding member and vice-president of the Pan African Society of Cardio-thoracic Surgeons, led the surgical team that implanted the hi-tech lifesaving HeartWare HVAD.

Summary:
In November last year, Philasande contracted a flu and within weeks his condition deteriorated. Turned out that he had the coxsachie virus and it affected his heart and valves so badly, he was dying. Doctors operated on him and he was given a temporary mechanical heart called the Tandem - pioneered by Milpark Hospital - to help his body heal.
Just a few weeks later, Philasande returned to the hospital and doctors realised he needed an immediate heart transplant. But at ten years old, he was too small to get a new heart and despite being placed on the Priority List for a heart, they couldn't find him one.

Dr Cassel, his attending cardiac specialist suggested that he be fitted with a Heartware Valve Assist Device (HVAD) - a mechanical heart - that up until then had never been fitted to a young child. He had to be flown to Cape Town to be operated on by Dr Willie Koen - the only surgeon on the continent who performs this operation - and Philasande received his new heart.

At the cost of R2million for the device and a total of R3million for the entire operation, doctors hope that the HVAD will keep Philasande going for the next few years until he is old enough to receive a heart big enough for his own body.

In the meantime, Philasande is back to being a happy healthy child.

Press Release:


Mechanical heart
Philasande Dladla was an ordinary ten-year-old Johannesburg boy until he contracted what seemed to be nothing more than the common flu virus. But suddenly diagnosed with acute heart failure, he faced a desperate fight for survival. In a first on the African continent, doctors managed to save his life by replacing his failing heart with not one, but two so-called mechanical hearts. Carte Blanche witnesses the miracle of modern medical technology at work.


Script:


VO: Ten year old Philasande Dladla, takes his first tentative steps around his hospital ward.
He’s spent weeks in the cardiac intensive care unit at the Christiaan Barnard Memorial Hospital in Cape Town, recovering from a second operation to implant a left ventricular assist device or a mechanical heart.
The only option left, to save his life.
LINK: Until late last year, Philasande Dladla was just an ordinary young boy who loved sports and spending time with his friends but all that changed when he contracted what his parents initially thought was nothing more than the common flu virus.
UPSOUND Phumlani Dladla TCR: 02:03:21:20:... He started like it was a normal flu,
UPSOUND Sindi Dladla TCR: 02:03:52:20: …It escalated to stomach craps, vomiting, all along we are thinking, it’s just a sickness, just a sickness.
VO: It turned out that Philasande had the coxsackie virus which, in most cases, causes mild flu-like symptoms. But in his case, it had far more devastating consequences.
His heart’s left ventricular chamber began to fail and as a result the heart muscle was under severe stress and his heart valves began to leak blood.
UPSOUND DR C TCR: 01:10:57:00 ......a large number of our transplant recipients have coxsachie virus beforehand and they they go and excersise and a week or a month later they become ill.
UPSOUND Sindi Dladla TCR: 02:03:52:20: ... the doctor ... he listened to the heart, and he’s like, there’s something wrong with his heart. He didn’t know what it was, but he said it’s swollen.
VO: Philasande was rushed by ambulance to Sunninghill hospital, where he was put on another machine to test his heart.
UPSOUND Sindi Dladla TCR: 02:03:52:20....he couldn’t walk from his bed to that machine. He couldn’t walk four steps....
We met Dr Yonka and he told us we have three days with him, he is dying. He said the organs are collapsing.
VO: In a desperate attempt to save his life, doctors at the hospital reached out to Dr Graham Cassel and Dr Agneta Geldenhuys, cardiologists from Milpark Hospital.
They devised a plan to implant a so-called ‘tandem heart’ device through his groin—a temporary mechanical heart to help Philasande’s failing organ.
UPSOUND Dr C TCR: 01:00:35:23: He was sent to us from another hospital for an emergency heart transplant and he arrived on a Friday afternoon and in simple terms, he wouldn’t have lived till Saturday morning.
UPSOUND Dr G TCR: 01:05:50:00: The tandem heart is the platform that we use for a short term left ventricular assist device, so basically if you can take blood before the failing chamber of the heart and give it back after the failing chamber, you take over the work of that chamber completely.
VO: The tandem heart allowed Philasande’s heart to recover and after a few days it was removed. Within weeks he was back at school but just six months later, his symptoms returned as he experienced stomach pains and vomiting, all over again.
UPSOUND Dr G TCR: 01:12:30:00: ... He’s got more and fluid fro his left heart failing, into his lungs so became more and more short of breath
his right heart started to fail because his left heart failed so the one thing led to the other.
UPSOUND Dr C TCR: 01:12:30:00:.... we spoke to the family within a couple of days and said the process had reversed itself, he’s not going to recover, he needs a transplant.
LINK: It’s notoriously difficult to find a new heart for children who need transplants and Philasande’s case was no different.
VO: He was immediately placed on the priority one list for a heart transplant but after six weeks in ICU, his chances for getting a new heart, were slim.
UPSOUND Dr C TCR: 01:01:11:00: One of our major problems world wide and specifically in SA is donor shortage and in this situation you’ve got to match size and blood group and he was a little boy who weighed just over 40 Kilos so donors of that size don’t come easily
VO: With a biological heart transplant now in serious doubt, Dr Cassel had just one more card left to play. He called on his colleague cardiac specialist Dr Willie Koen in Cape Town to assist.
UPSOUND Dr Koen TCR: 03:45:46:08
Artificial hearts is a fairly new concept and currently it’s mainly for adults and in children, it is not a common procedure, but when we heard the urgency of Philasande and we asked about his size, his body weight and then we realised that this is a potential patient that we can actually extend the invitation for a child.
UPSOUND Sindi Dladla TCR: 02:18:50:00… He told us that there is a mechanical heart available in CPT and it costs R2million he’s going to put in a motivation to the medical aid and see if they approve…
I remember I was with Philasande in hospital Dr Cassel came in and he just said, the medical aid didn’t approve.
VO: Philasande needed to be fitted with the more permanent Left Ventricular Heart Assist device also known as the LVAD, at the total cost of R3.2 million. The family’s medical aid, Best Med, led by CEO Dries Le Grange had the difficult job of deciding Philasande’s fate.
UPSOUND CEO Dries le Grange TCR: 42:05:22:00
the cost effectiveness is something we have to strive for, we don’t have money that will fall out of the sky because of new technology that comes into the market.
VO: But Sindi persisted and taking into account Dr Willie Koen’s advice, Best Med agreed to pay.
UPSOUND CEO TCR: 42:41:16
..I think what made us change our mind was Dr Willie Koen who shared wonderful information and he shared with us that they will implant the device and the device will remain there for at least six years
VO: Once the team received the greenlight from the medical aid, Philasande and his mother, were immediately airlifted to Cape Town’s Christiaan Barnard Memorial Hospital.
LINK: In 1967, Dr Chris Barnard performed the first successful human heart transplant at the Groot Schuur Hospital in Cape Town then in 2000, the first mechanical heart transplant to successfully take place on the African continent, was performed here at Christiaan Barnard Memorial Hospital.
VO Cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Willie Koen, led the team which performed that very first operation in the year 2000 and he was also on hand to receive Philasande when he arrived, in critical condition.
UPSOUND Dr Koen TCR: 03:47:11:24
We realised he was sick but when he arrived here and we saw how sick he was, we realised that this child needed something to be done very soon.
UPSOUND Dr Koen: He was so overloaded with fluid I mean his hands and feet were swollen because his heart can’t pump the blood so it just accumulates in his legs, in his abdomen, in his face.
VO: The LVAD is designed to take stress from the heart to help it pump more blood but with less effort.
Blood flows from the left ventricle into the device and it pumps the blood out into the aorta, where it then flows to the rest of the body.

UPSOUND Dr Koen TCR: 03:51:25:00 ...We open the tip of the heart and we insert the tip of this device into the left ventricle and then we must tunnel underneath the patients skin, a small tunnel, to bring the electric cable out and that will be connected to the battery.



VO: Each power unit lasts between four to seven hours and Philasande and his father, have taken on the responsibility of changing his batteries.
Philasande admits that his first attempt at a battery change, was a daunting experience.
UPSOUND Philasande TCR: 03:03:13:22
I was shaking, I was scared like, I couldn’t do it...it felt like that is my life, so if I take it something wrong, something that I do that is wrong, then I will die.So I was shaking every time.
VO: The family has had to adapt while Philasande recovers at home for the rest of the year. And his parents are still looking for a new school for him for the new year.
UPSOUND Philasande TCR: 03:05:07:13
Sometimes when I wore it the first time, it was heavy but now I’m used to it, it just feels like I’m wearing a bag.
UPSOUND Sindi Dladla TCR: 02:43;06:13 Every parent wants to see their son or kids, living a normal healthy life. ... ofcourse this is a miracle and we are grateful, grateful is even an understatement that we have this, but having a heart will be great.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Philasande Dladla became the first child on the African continent to undergo a lifesaving operation where a “mechanical heart” was implanted to assist his damaged heart. He is also the first child in the world to have a mechanical heart implanted in him. Doctors at the Netcare Christiaan Barnard Memorial Hospital in Cape Town inserted a heart ventricular assist device (HVAD) in Dladla aged 10 from KwaZulu-Natal. Dr Willie Koen, a cardiac and transplant surgeon practising at the hospital, and a founding member and vice-president of the Pan African Society of Cardio-thoracic Surgeons, led the surgical team that implanted the hi-tech lifesaving HeartWare HVAD.
metadata.Summary: In November last year, Philasande contracted a flu and within weeks his condition deteriorated. Turned out that he had the coxsachie virus and it affected his heart and valves so badly, he was dying. Doctors operated on him and he was given a temporary mechanical heart called the Tandem - pioneered by Milpark Hospital - to help his body heal. Just a few weeks later, Philasande returned to the hospital and doctors realised he needed an immediate heart transplant. But at ten years old, he was too small to get a new heart and despite being placed on the Priority List for a heart, they couldn't find him one. Dr Cassel, his attending cardiac specialist suggested that he be fitted with a Heartware Valve Assist Device (HVAD) - a mechanical heart - that up until then had never been fitted to a young child. He had to be flown to Cape Town to be operated on by Dr Willie Koen - the only surgeon on the continent who performs this operation - and Philasande received his new heart. At the cost of R2million for the device and a total of R3million for the entire operation, doctors hope that the HVAD will keep Philasande going for the next few years until he is old enough to receive a heart big enough for his own body. In the meantime, Philasande is back to being a happy healthy child.
